items.title: The weekly eyewash check: a routine that holds up
items.excerpt: The weekly activation is the simplest check in Z358.1 and the easiest to let slip. Here's what it's for, a six step routine for plumbed and self contained units, and how to log it so it stands up at audit.
items.cover_alt: A green combination safety shower and eyewash station on a grated floor in a process plant
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Of all the checks in ANSI Z358.1, the weekly one is the simplest and the easiest to let slip. It doesn't need a contractor or a specialist. It needs someone to walk to each unit, run it and write it down. I built Z358 One to make that last step easy to do and hard to lose.

This is what the weekly check is for, a routine that fits into a normal working week, and how to keep a record that stands up to an audit. The equipment itself sits in our [Emergency division](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/).

## What the weekly activation is for

[Bradley's quick compliance guide to Z358.1](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) says emergency drench showers, eyewashes and eye and face washes must be activated once a week. It gives two reasons. The activation makes sure nothing is blocking the flow, and it eliminates any chance of contamination from stagnant water. [Bradley's guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) adds that it clears sediment in the supply line.

Think about who gets that water. Someone with a chemical in their eyes gets whatever has been sitting in the pipe since the last time the unit ran.

The weekly check proves the unit works today. It doesn't replace the annual inspection, which [ANSI recommends](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) to evaluate changes to the workspace, assess new hazards and identify fixtures that need repair or replacement. If you want the bigger picture on where sites fall down, I covered it in [the eyewash and shower checks that fail audits](https://aquelon.com/insights/ansi-z358-1-eyewash-and-shower-checks-that-fail-audits).

## Plumbed or self contained

The routine depends on the unit. Plumbed units get activated. [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) says they should be run long enough to be sure flushing fluid is provided.

Self contained units are different. [The same guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) says they don't need activating, but they do need a visual inspection to check there's enough flushing fluid, and its weekly checklist says they must be inspected every week to make sure they're ready for use. For fluid changes and cleaning, follow the manufacturer's instructions, which [Bradley notes](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) should be readily available to maintenance and training staff.

## A routine that fits a normal week

Do the same things in the same order at every unit, every week:

1. **Walk the route.** Start at the hazard and walk to the unit. [Bradley's weekly checklist](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) says to remove any obstructions or trip hazards, and to be aware that a door may be considered an obstruction.
2. **Look at the unit.** Replace any broken or missing parts straight away, as [the checklist](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) puts it. Check the eyewash heads are protected from contaminants, which [Bradley's quick guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) lists as a requirement. Check the sign is still [highly visible and the area is adequately lit](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf).
3. **Run it, if it's plumbed.** The valve should [open in one second or less and stay open until it's closed by hand](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149). If someone has to hold it open, that's a fail. On a self contained unit, this is where you check the fluid level instead.
4. **Check the temperature.** [Bradley's checklist](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) includes testing the water with an industrial thermometer to make sure it's tepid, which the guide defines as 16 to 38°C (60 to 100°F). In Gulf heat this one matters, and I went through the options in [tempered water for safety showers](https://aquelon.com/insights/tempered-water-for-safety-showers-in-gulf-heat).
5. **Deal with the water.** A shower releases a lot of it. [Bradley's quick guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) warns that pooling flushing fluid creates slip hazards, so have a drain or a container ready before you open the valve.
6. **Write it down.** [The checklist](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) says to document activations on the unit's inspection tag and in any central log.

## Logging it so it counts

An activation nobody recorded is hard to prove at audit. [Bradley's quick guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) notes that inspection tags often come with the fixture to document testing and to satisfy a safety audit. A tag on the unit is a good start. A central record is better, because it shows the pattern across every unit and every week.

Record the same things each time: the unit, the date, who did it, pass or fail, and what was wrong if it failed. A failed check needs an action and a date against it, not just a cross on a tag.

That's the job [Z358 One](https://z358one.com/) was built for. It logs each weekly activation against the registered unit, with the inspector's name, date, pass or fail and deficiency notes, permanently timestamped. It also sends alerts when a weekly activation is overdue, so a missed week shows up before the auditor finds it.

Two things keep the routine alive. Give every unit a named owner, and give the check a fixed day. Pay particular attention to units in plant rooms and outdoor areas that nobody walks past.

## The short version

Run every plumbed unit every week to clear stagnant water and prove the flow. Visually inspect self contained units every week. Walk the route, look at the unit, run it, check the temperature, manage the water and write it down. Keep a central record, not just a tag.

Specifying or replacing emergency equipment? [Send the scope or BOQ](https://aquelon.com/quote/) and we'll come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- Bradley Corporation, "ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Quick Compliance Guide". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149
- Bradley Corporation, "A Guide to the ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Standard for Emergency Eyewashes and Shower Equipment", 2024. https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf

items.title: Tempered water for safety showers in Gulf heat
items.excerpt: Z358.1 asks for tepid water, 16 to 38°C, for the full 15 minute flush. In Gulf heat, an exposed supply line can run far hotter. Here's why, and the options that keep a safety shower in range all summer.
items.cover_alt: A green combination safety shower and eyewash station on a grated floor in a process plant
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
I grew Hughes Safety Showers from £3.9M to £6.9M and built Z358 One to record eyewash and shower inspections. Flow rates and reach distances are easy to put on a drawing. Water temperature is harder, because it changes with the weather, and in Gulf heat it's the requirement most exposed to the sun.

This is what the standard asks for, why outdoor lines run hot, and the options that keep a safety shower in range all summer. The equipment itself sits in our [Emergency division](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/).

## What tepid actually means

[ANSI/ISEA Z358.1](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/) says emergency showers and eyewashes should deliver tepid flushing fluid, and puts tepid at 16 to 38°C. The European series sets its own range: [Hughes' summary](https://www.hughes-safety.com/gb/hub/tepid-water-importance-in-safety-showers/) gives 15 to 37°C for EN 15154. Check which standard your project names, and what the operator or authority on your site expects.

The range isn't about comfort for its own sake. [Bradley's quick compliance guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) says tepid water is required to encourage the injured person to keep flushing for the full 15 minutes. [Bradley's guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) adds that temperatures above 100°F may cause chemical interactions with the skin and result in further damage. [Hughes adds](https://www.hughes-safety.com/gb/hub/tepid-water-importance-in-safety-showers/) that if the water is too hot, the casualty may leave the shower early with the chemical still on them.

## Why exposed lines run hot

A plumbed shower holds standing water in its pipework between uses, which is why [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) ties the weekly activation to clearing stagnant water. Outdoors in a Gulf summer, that water sits in the sun. [Hughes notes](https://www.hughes-safety.com/gb/hub/tepid-water-importance-in-safety-showers/) that exposed pipework in direct sunlight can heat water to above 50°C, risking burns. That's the first water the casualty gets.

Volume matters too. [Bradley's guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) points out that a compliant showerhead releasing 20 US gallons a minute delivers 300 gallons over 15 minutes, roughly 1,140 litres. That's the quantity you need to keep tepid, not just the first few seconds. On a combination unit, [the same guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) says to assume every drenching system may be activated at once, and the system must still deliver an uninterrupted, tepid 15 minute flush.

## The options for keeping it tepid

**Chilled tank showers.** Where the supply is unreliable or the line runs hot, a tank fed shower with cooling holds its own volume. The [Hughes 1500 litre jacketed and insulated tank shower](https://aquelon.com/products/hughes-exp-j-14ks-1500/) has chiller options for hot climates, including the Hughes Zero Power Cooler. The [ISTEC overhead tank shower](https://aquelon.com/products/ist-type-esw-owt-630/) takes an optional immersion heater or chiller to hold the water between 15 and 38°C, with low water level and water temperature alarms.

**Self draining units.** Another route is to stop water standing in the sun at all. The [ISTEC self draining combination unit](https://aquelon.com/products/ist-type-esw-sd/) empties after each use and is designed to be scald proof. [Hughes points out](https://www.hughes-safety.com/gb/hub/tepid-water-importance-in-safety-showers/) that self draining showers need a tepid mains supply, so this only works where the supply itself is in range.

**Thermostatic mixing valves.** A mixing valve blends two supplies to a set temperature. The [Acorn ET71 emergency mixing valve](https://aquelon.com/products/acorn-et71-1-bvs-otg/) is factory set to 30°C with an adjustable maximum of 35°C, and is rated at 37.1 litres per minute at 30 PSID. That covers the [minimum eyewash and eye and face wash flows](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) of 1.5 and 11 litres a minute, but it's under half the 76 litres a minute a shower needs, so size the valve to the fixture it feeds. Acorn's [Command Station](https://aquelon.com/products/acorn-cset/) packages the ET71 into a tempering station. Remember a mixing valve can only blend what it's given. If neither supply is below 38°C, it can't produce tepid water on its own, so pair it with a cooled source.

**Shade and insulation.** Shade the unit and insulate exposed runs where you can. Treat them as support for one of the options above, not a fix on their own.

## Testing in summer

[Bradley's weekly checklist](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) includes testing the water temperature with an industrial thermometer to make sure it's tepid. A simple routine:

- Measure at the outlet, not in the plant room.
- Test in the hottest part of the day during the hottest months, because that's when the unit is most likely to be out of range.
- Record the first reading and the reading once the line has run. If the first water is hot, you know how long the casualty waits for tepid.
- Log it per unit. [Z358 One](https://z358one.com/) records weekly activations and annual inspections, including temperature measurement at the annual check, in a timestamped record.

The right setpoint also depends on the chemical. [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) recommends consulting a safety or health advisor, because no two hazards are exactly the same.

## What to put in the specification

- The standard and tepid range the project uses: ANSI Z358.1 or the relevant part of EN 15154
- A tempering method sized for the full 15 minute flow in peak summer conditions, for every outlet that can run at once
- Mixing valve flow ratings checked against each fixture's minimum flow
- Water temperature alarms on tank systems where they're offered
- Outlet temperature readings at commissioning, recorded per unit
- A weekly and annual inspection regime that includes temperature

## The short version

Tepid is 16 to 38°C under Z358.1. In Gulf heat, the water standing in an exposed line can be well above that. Pick a tempering method that covers the full flow, check valve ratings against the fixture, and test at the outlet when it's hottest.

Specifying or upgrading emergency showers for a hot site? [Send the scope or BOQ](https://aquelon.com/quote/) and we'll come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- American National Standards Institute, "ANSI Z358.1-2014: Emergency Eyewash and Shower Standard", 2018. https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/
- Bradley Corporation, "ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Quick Compliance Guide". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149
- Bradley Corporation, "A Guide to the ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Standard for Emergency Eyewashes and Shower Equipment", 2024. https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf
- Hughes Safety Showers, "The Importance of Tepid Water in Emergency Safety Showers". https://www.hughes-safety.com/gb/hub/tepid-water-importance-in-safety-showers/

items.title: AISI 304 or 316: choosing stainless steel for Gulf coastal sites
items.excerpt: Near the sea, the stainless steel grade on the datasheet decides how outdoor water equipment looks a few summers on. Here's when 316 should be the starting point, why finish and cleaning matter as much as grade, and what to write into the spec.
items.cover_alt: A stainless steel drinking fountain beside a running track in a Gulf city park at sunset
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
If you're specifying stainless steel for a site near the sea, the grade on the datasheet decides how the kit looks a few summers from now. Drinking fountains, bottle fillers, hand wash stations and safety showers all sit out in salt air on waterfront projects. Here's how I'd make the call between AISI 304 and 316, and what I'd write into the spec.

## What actually separates 304 and 316

The [Australian Stainless Steel Development Association](https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up) (ASSDA) puts it simply. Grade 316 has "virtually the same mechanical, physical and fabrication characteristics as 304 with better corrosion resistance, particularly to pitting corrosion in chloride environments". It calls 316 the first step up from 304, and says it's often chosen for sea front buildings and fittings on wharves and piers.

The difference comes from the alloy. ASSDA's composition table gives 316 between 2.0 and 3.0% molybdenum. Its [guidance on coastal corrosion](https://www.assda.asn.au/publications/technical-faqs/preventing-coastal-corrosion-tea-staining) explains that additions such as molybdenum and nitrogen improve corrosion resistance, especially where chlorides are present.

## How close to the water is too close

The problem you'll see first is tea staining: brown discolouration of the surface by corrosion. ASSDA is clear that it's cosmetic and doesn't affect the structural integrity or lifetime of the steel. On a fountain in a public park, though, cosmetic still matters. A stained unit looks neglected.

ASSDA's guide says tea staining is most likely up to five kilometres from a surf beach and one kilometre from still marine waters. Wind exposure, pollution, sheltering and higher temperatures can push that to 20 kilometres or more, and tropical and high humidity areas are more at risk. Its recommendation is that grade 316, or a grade with equivalent corrosion resistance, should be the minimum within five kilometres of the surf. The lower grades such as 304 will probably stain or corrode more seriously in a marine environment.

So for a corniche, a marina, a beach park or a waterfront school, I'd treat 316 as the starting point, not the upgrade. Indoors is different. ASSDA notes tea staining is rarely a problem indoors because of the low humidity and the absence of corrosive deposits, so 304 is a sensible choice for indoor units.

## Grade alone won't save a bad finish

This is where specs fall short. ASSDA strongly recommends a surface roughness under 0.5 µm Ra, and says specifying a No. 4 finish is inadequate without stating the roughness you need. Rough grooves trap salt, and the salt does the damage.

Design matters too. Surfaces should drain freely and be exposed to rain washing. Horizontal surfaces that pond water and areas sheltered from rain are where staining gets worse. For splash zones, unwashed areas or rough surfaces, ASSDA says higher grades such as duplex may be required. Welds need their heat tint removed and the surface passivated, for example by pickling.

Then there's cleaning. ASSDA's advice is to wash with soap or mild detergent and warm water, then rinse with clean cold water. Abrasive cleaners and anything containing chlorides or bleach mustn't be used, and hydrochloric acid is out too, because it stains the surface and usually starts more serious corrosion. If the site's cleaning contractor uses bleach on everything, your 316 won't stay looking like 316.

## Powder coat as an option

Some projects want colour. On our powder coated models we can supply any RAL Classic colour, and I'd always get a physical swatch signed off before order. Treat the coating as a colour choice, not a substitute for the grade. Ask what sits under it and what the parts people touch are made of. The [Murdock GRM45](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-grm45/) bi level pedestal, for example, comes in satin stainless steel or a powder coated finish, and its bowls are 304 stainless steel. That's worth knowing before it goes on a sea front.

## What to write in the spec

- The grade for each part: body, pedestal, bowl and any panels. One grade on the cover sheet isn't enough.
- 316 or equivalent as the minimum within five kilometres of the surf, with a higher grade considered for splash zones and unwashed areas.
- Surface roughness under 0.5 µm Ra, not just "No. 4".
- Welds cleaned and passivated.
- A cleaning instruction in the handover: mild detergent, warm water, clean rinse, no bleach, chlorides or abrasives.

Some equipment already offers the choice. The IST [Type ES pedestal emergency shower](https://aquelon.com/products/ist-type-es/) and the [Type EW eye and face wash](https://aquelon.com/products/ist-type-ew/) both have separate part numbers for AISI 304 and AISI 316. For hydration, the EMSAS [ECS outdoor fountain](https://aquelon.com/products/emsas-ecs/) has a 316 grade stainless steel body. Ask for the grade by part number on the submittal, then check it on delivery.

## The short version

- 316 resists pitting in chloride environments better than 304. Near the sea, that's what you're paying for.
- ASSDA says tea staining is most likely within five kilometres of a surf beach and one kilometre of still marine water, and can reach further in heat and humidity.
- Indoors, 304 is usually fine.
- Specify roughness under 0.5 µm Ra, drainage, weld treatment and a cleaning regime, not just the grade.
- Powder coat is for colour. Check the grade underneath and the bowls.

Our [Hydration](https://aquelon.com/divisions/hydration/) and [Emergency](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/) ranges both carry 316 options. Send the scope or BOQ at [aquelon.com/quote](https://aquelon.com/quote/) and we'll come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- Australian Stainless Steel Development Association, "316: The First Step Up". https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up
- Australian Stainless Steel Development Association, "FAQ 6: Preventing Coastal Corrosion (Tea Staining)". https://www.assda.asn.au/publications/technical-faqs/preventing-coastal-corrosion-tea-staining

items.title: Bottle fillers or drinking fountains: which does your site need?
items.excerpt: Drinking fountains and bottle fillers serve different people. Here is when each one fits, why combination units suit most sites, and what the 2021 International Plumbing Code says about the mix.
items.cover_alt: A woman filling a bottle at a stainless steel pedestal combining a bottle filler and a drinking fountain in a sunlit city plaza
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Drinking fountains, bottle fillers, or both? It's a question every hydration scope has to answer. The answer comes down to who uses the space, how they drink and what your plumbing code asks for. Here's how I'd work through it.

## What each one is actually for

A drinking fountain is for a quick drink on the spot. The [International Plumbing Code](https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IPC2021P1/chapter-2-definitions) defines it as a fixture that lets the user "obtain a drink directly from a stream of flowing water without the use of any accessories".

A bottle filler fills a container. The same code covers that as a water dispenser, a fixture for dispensing drinking water "into a receptacle such as a cup, glass or bottle".

That difference drives everything else. A fountain serves someone walking past who wants a drink now. A filler serves someone who'll carry their water with them for the next few hours.

## When a fountain fits and when a filler fits

Fountains suit short, frequent visits from people who don't carry a bottle. Think playgrounds at break time, sports pitches, park paths and the corridor outside a classroom. Nobody has to remember anything. They walk up and drink.

Bottle fillers suit people who stay put and keep water at their desk or in their bag. Offices, universities, gyms, airport gates and hospital staff areas all fit that pattern. A laminar stream fills a bottle cleanly. The [Murdock BF12S](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf12s/), for example, delivers a laminar flow at 1.2 gallons per minute.

Most sites have both kinds of user, which is why the answer is so often both.

## The case for combination units

A combination unit puts a bowl and a bottle filler on one fixture. One position on the drawing, one supply, one waste.

Indoors, the [Topserw A171 BF](https://aquelon.com/products/topserw-a171-bf/) has separate self closing buttons or sensors for the fountain and the filler, and it's designed only for indoor applications. Outdoors, the [Murdock GYM74](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-gym74/) is a stainless steel pedestal with a pushbutton fountain and a pushbutton or sensor operated filler.

If you want chilled water outside, read the installation notes. The notes for Murdock's [outdoor pedestal unit with a chiller](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-mgym74-a021/) say best practice is installation beneath an overhang, avoiding direct sunlight. In a Gulf summer that's not optional detail, it belongs on the drawing.

Two more worth knowing about. For parks where people walk dogs, there's a [pedestal bottle filler with a pet fountain](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-m-obf4-pf/) receptor. For mental health settings, a [ligature resistant fountain with bottle filler](https://aquelon.com/products/topserw-m-dfbf-lr/) uses tapered side splashes, sloping tops and a conical bubbler to reduce ligature points.

## What the code says about the mix

If your project follows the [2021 International Plumbing Code](https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings), three clauses shape the choice.

- **Section 410.4.** Where three or more drinking fountains are required, water dispensers can be substituted for not more than 50 percent of the required number. Bottle fillers can't replace every fountain on the count.
- **Sections 410.3 and 410.3.1.** Where fountains are provided on an exterior site, on a floor or within a secured area, there must be at least two: one for people who use a wheelchair and one for standing persons. A single fountain with two separate spouts that serves both can be substituted.
- **Section 410.5.** Drinking fountains, water coolers and water dispensers "shall not be installed in public restrooms".

If you're looking at bi level units such as the [Murdock GRE24](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-gre24/), ask for the dimensions and check them against your authority's accessibility requirements.

Check which code your authority applies, and any local amendments, before you fix the count.

## Hygiene and how people use them

Start with touch. Several of the units above offer sensor operation on the filler, so nobody has to press a button to fill a bottle. Decide sensor or pushbutton per location, not per project.

Then think about maintenance. The [Topserw BF15 and BF16 range](https://aquelon.com/products/topserw-bf15/) offers a BCD version with a bottle counter and a filter replacement display. That gives whoever looks after the unit a visible prompt, rather than a date in a spreadsheet nobody opens.

Placement decides use. Put units where people already walk, keep them out of restrooms and keep the area around them easy to clean. A filler tucked behind a stairwell won't get used, whatever it cost.

## The short version

- Fountains for quick drinks from people without a bottle.
- Bottle fillers for people who stay on site and carry water.
- Combination units where you have both, which is most sites.
- Under the 2021 IPC, dispensers replace no more than half where three or more fountains are required, and nothing goes in a public restroom. Check what your authority applies.
- Read the installation notes on chilled outdoor units. Murdock's says beneath an overhang, out of direct sunlight.

You'll find the full [Hydration range](https://aquelon.com/divisions/hydration/) on our site. Send the scope or BOQ at [aquelon.com/quote](https://aquelon.com/quote/) and we'll come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- International Code Council, "2021 International Plumbing Code, Chapter 2 Definitions", 2021. https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IPC2021P1/chapter-2-definitions
- International Code Council, "2021 International Plumbing Code, Chapter 4 Fixtures, Faucets and Fixture Fittings", 2021. https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings

items.title: Counting the bottles: what a refill station actually saves
items.excerpt: On these planning assumptions, a refill programme for 600 people replaces 150,000 plastic bottles a year. Here is the arithmetic, the estimates behind it, and how to adapt them to your own site.
items.cover_alt: A stainless steel drinking fountain beside a running track in a Gulf city park at sunset
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Refill stations are one of the easier places to put a number on a sustainability goal. The sum is simple, and you can test every assumption behind it.

Here is the arithmetic, with the assumptions on the table.

## The basic sum

Bottles avoided in a year is people on site, times refills per person per day, times days the site is open.

Take an office with 600 people, each refilling once a day, open on weekdays only, about 250 days a year. A school will have fewer open days, so use its own calendar.

600 × 1 × 250 = **150,000 bottles a year.**

That assumes everyone takes part and every refill replaces one bought 500 ml bottle. Lower take up gives a lower number, so adjust it for your site.

## Turning bottles into plastic, carbon and money

These are the planning assumptions we use in the [calculator on our homepage](https://aquelon.com/#impact). They are estimates, not certified figures, and you should swap in your own if you have them.

| Assumption | Value we use |
| --- | --- |
| PET in a 500 ml bottle | 10 g |
| Carbon per bottle, production to disposal | 80 g CO₂e |
| Price per bottle | AED 1.00 |

On 150,000 bottles that comes to:

- **1.5 tonnes** of PET plastic that never gets made, shipped or thrown away
- **12 tonnes** of CO₂e avoided
- **AED 150,000** of bottled water spend replaced

These are gross figures. They make no allowance for the electricity, water or equipment the refill station itself uses.

Double the refills to two a day and every number doubles. Open seven days a week, as a hospital, airport or mall does, and multiply by 365 instead of 250.

## Why this matters for reporting

[LEED](https://www.usgbc.org/leed) covers water use, materials and waste, and Abu Dhabi's [Estidama Pearl Rating System](https://www.dmt.gov.ae/en/adm/Media-Centre/News/08Jan2025) assesses buildings against sustainability requirements. Neither scheme is a reason to assume a refill programme earns credit. What it gives you is a number to put against goals on water, materials and waste, so check which credits or targets your project is actually going for.

Two things make the number stronger.

**Measure it.** [Some bottle filling stations](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf16s/) have an optional bottle counter display. A counter replaces the refill assumption with actual use. The plastic, carbon and cost figures remain estimates.

**Make it easy.** Usage follows convenience. Put refill stations where people already walk, chill the water, and make sure there is no queue. A unit tucked behind a stairwell does not move the number.

## Where the savings are biggest

The sites with the most people per day win: [airports and metro stations](https://aquelon.com/sectors/airports-transit/), [universities and large schools](https://aquelon.com/sectors/education/), [hospitals](https://aquelon.com/sectors/healthcare/) and [stadiums](https://aquelon.com/sectors/sports-leisure/). For a stadium, work the sum per event as well as per year.

## Run your own numbers

Our [impact calculator](https://aquelon.com/#impact) does this sum for sites of 50 to 5,000 people in a few seconds and shows the assumptions underneath it. Put in your head count, refills and opening days, and use the result in your business case.

If you want help sizing a refill programme for a specific site, [send the floor plan and the occupancy](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- US Green Building Council, "LEED rating system". https://www.usgbc.org/leed
- Abu Dhabi City Municipality, "Abu Dhabi City Municipality Promotes Sustainable Green Building Concept and Projects", 8 January 2025. https://www.dmt.gov.ae/en/adm/Media-Centre/News/08Jan2025

items.title: ANSI Z358.1 in plain English: the eyewash and shower checks that fail audits
items.excerpt: A unit that met the standard on the day it was installed can still fail an audit later. Here are five common reasons, with the numbers that matter.
items.cover_alt: A green combination safety shower and eyewash station on a grated floor in a process plant
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
I grew Hughes Safety Showers from £3.9M to £6.9M, and I built Z358 One to record eyewash and shower inspections. A unit that met the standard on the day it went in can still fail later. Here are five common ways that happens.

[ANSI/ISEA Z358.1](https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/) is the American national standard for emergency eyewash and shower equipment. EN 15154 is the European series, with parts including [laboratory body showers](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025) and [plumbed in eyewash units](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025), so check which part your project names. This is the plain English version of what the American standard asks for, and where sites fall down. The equipment itself sits in our [Emergency division](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/).

## The numbers that matter

The full standard is a paid document from its publisher. These figures come from [Bradley's quick compliance guide to Z358.1](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149), which gives the section number for each, with the temperature range from [ANSI's own summary](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/) and the annual check from [Bradley's guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf).

| Requirement | What Z358.1 asks for |
| --- | --- |
| Reach | Within 10 seconds of the hazard, with 16.8 metres as the guideline, on the same level |
| Activation | Valve opens in one second or less and stays open until closed by hand |
| Eyewash flow | At least 1.5 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Eye and face wash flow | At least 11 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Shower flow | At least 76 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Water temperature | Tepid, about 16°C to 38°C |
| Shower head height | Between 208 cm and 244 cm above the floor |
| Spray pattern | At least 50.8 cm across at 152 cm above the floor |
| Weekly check | Activate every plumbed unit to clear the line and confirm flow |
| Annual check | Inspect every unit each year to confirm it complies |

Those numbers are the easy part. Keeping a site inside them is the hard part.

## Fail one: the water is too hot

Heat is the obvious risk in the Gulf. [The standard says tepid](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/), with 16 to 38°C as the range. An exposed supply line in summer can take the first minutes of flow above that, and [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) notes that environmental conditions often require freeze or scald protection. Tepid is there for a reason: [the same guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) says it is to encourage the injured person to keep flushing for the full 15 minutes.

The fix is designed in, not bolted on. Specify a tempered water system sized for the full flow: a chiller or a [tank shower with a chiller option](https://aquelon.com/products/hughes-exp-j-14ks-1500/). A [thermostatic mixing valve](https://aquelon.com/products/acorn-et71-1-bvs-otg/) can suit eyewash flows, but check its rated flow against the unit, and remember it can only blend the water it is given. Insulate and shade the supply line. Then test the temperature at the outlet in July, not in January.

## Fail two: something is in the way

The route to the unit has to be clear and on the same level. Ten seconds is not long. A pallet, a hose reel or a new piece of plant parked in front of the shower breaks that, and so can a door added after commissioning. [A door counts as an obstruction](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149). The one exception is a single unlocked door that opens in the direction of travel, and only where the contaminant is not hazardous or corrosive.

Walk the route from each hazard, time it, and repeat it every time the layout changes.

## Fail three: nobody runs it weekly

The weekly activation of a plumbed unit does two jobs. It proves nothing is blocking the flow, and it clears the stagnant water sitting in the pipe, which [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) names as a contamination risk. That standing water is what the injured worker gets first.

[Self contained units do not need activating, but they do need a visual inspection](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf).

Give every unit a named owner, and log the check. [Z358 One](https://z358one.com/) exists for that job: weekly activations and annual inspections are timestamped and stored in a compliance record, instead of living on a clipboard.

## Fail four: flow is below the minimum

Pressure drops as a site grows. A shower that delivered 76 litres per minute at commissioning can fall below the line once new users are added to the same main. Eyewash nozzles also scale up and partially block, especially with hard water.

Measure it properly. For eyewash units, [Bradley's guide](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149) calls for a flow meter for the flow rate and a test gauge for the spray pattern. For showers, [its guide to the standard](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf) describes a drench shower tester with a bucket to contain the water and measure it against the 20 US gallons per minute minimum. Do not eyeball it. Protect eyewash heads from contaminants and keep the nozzles clean.

## Fail five: you cannot see it

The standard calls for a [highly visible sign close to the unit and adequate lighting around it](https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf). Signs fade in UV, get painted over during shutdowns and get hidden by new cabling. A worker with chemicals in their eyes is not reading small print. Check the signage and lighting at every annual inspection.

## What to put in the specification

If you are writing a spec for a new facility, ask for:

- Units independently evaluated by a third party against the standard your project names, ANSI Z358.1 or the relevant part of EN 15154
- A tempered water solution sized for 15 minutes of full flow at peak summer supply temperature
- Scald protection for the heat, and freeze protection only where it is genuinely needed
- Stainless or coated finishes suited to the chemicals on site
- Flow and temperature test results at commissioning, recorded per unit
- Data sheets and certificates for the submittal pack
- A weekly and annual inspection regime handed over with the equipment

## The short version

Compliant on day one is not the same as compliant on audit day. Control the temperature. Keep the route clear. Run every plumbed unit every week. Measure flow once a year. Make sure people can see it.

If you are specifying or replacing emergency equipment, [send the layout and the hazard list](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- International Safety Equipment Association, "American National Standard for Emergency Eyewash and Shower Equipment", ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 (R2020). https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/
- Bradley Corporation, "ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Quick Compliance Guide". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/26149
- Bradley Corporation, "A Guide to the ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Standard for Emergency Eyewashes and Shower Equipment". https://media.bradleycorp.com/view/20293/Bradley_Safety_ANSIGuide.pdf
- American National Standards Institute, "ANSI Z358.1-2014: Emergency Eyewash and Shower Standard". https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-1:2025, Plumbed-in body showers for laboratories", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-2:2025, Plumbed-in eyewash units", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025

items.title: Specifying drinking fountains for GCC schools: what to put in the tender
items.excerpt: A school fountain in the Gulf has to cope with heat, salt air and heavy daily use. Here is what I would write into the specification so the units you approve are the right ones for the site.
items.cover_alt: Two pupils drinking from stainless steel pedestal fountains under a shade canopy in a school courtyard
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
A drinking fountain looks like the simplest line on a school BOQ, but the problems that show up later are usually written in at specification stage. Warm water, blocked bubblers and units that cannot take the sun all start with what went into the tender.

I have spent about 30 years in industrial equipment sales, so here is what I would put in the tender for a [school in the GCC](https://aquelon.com/sectors/education/).

## Start with the number of units, not the model

Decide how many outlets the site needs before anyone picks a product. Table 403.1 of the International Plumbing Code is a useful starting point. [The 2021 edition of the table](https://codes.iccsafe.org/s/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings/IPC2021P1-Ch04-Sec403.1) sets one drinking fountain per 100 occupants for educational facilities. Check what your authority actually adopts, because it varies by emirate and by country.

Then think about where pupils are, not just how many. Break times bring large numbers of pupils into the same place at once, and outlets grouped at the far end of a corridor can meet the ratio and still leave a queue. Put outlets where the crowds form: playgrounds, sports halls, canteens and the main circulation routes.

## Write the climate into the specification

A unit that performs well in a mild climate is not automatically fit for a Riyadh playground in August, so write the site conditions into the specification.

- **Chilled water where pupils actually drink.** Outdoor pipework in direct sun heats the water standing in it, and warm water is less inviting to drink. Specify a chiller or a [chilled bottle filler](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-mgym74-a021/) for the main outlets, and confirm shade and a power supply before you approve it. For that unit the guidance is to install it beneath an overhang away from direct sunlight, and continual ambient temperatures above 80°F (about 27°C) may wear the compressor prematurely. Ask for the same guidance on any chilled unit you are offered.
- **Stainless steel grade.** Near the sea, consider AISI 316 rather than 304. It has [better resistance to pitting in chloride environments](https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up). If you prefer a powder coated finish, ask the manufacturer what coastal exposure it is warranted for.
- **Powder coat to a RAL reference.** If the architect wants colour, write the RAL number into the spec and ask for a physical sample before approval. Screen colours lie.

## Design for heavy use and abuse

Schools are hard on equipment, so write robustness into the specification.

- Vandal resistant bubblers with a protective guard, so mouths never touch the outlet.
- Push buttons that are mechanical and self closing, or sensor operation if the budget allows. Avoid twist taps.
- Fixings that cannot be undone with a coin or a ruler.
- Units bolted to a proper base or wall, not just sealed to the floor.

## Make it accessible

Specify at least one accessible outlet at every location. A [dual height unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-grm45/) gives a lower bowl for wheelchair users and younger pupils and a standard height bowl for older pupils and staff. Check the lower bowl height against your youngest age group. Ask for the clear knee space and the reach range to be shown on the datasheet. [Section 602 of the ADA Standards](https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602) is a useful benchmark. It covers knee and toe clearance, operable parts and spout height.

## Put bottle fillers in the mix

If pupils carry reusable bottles, a bottle filling station handles that better than a bubbler, and [some units have a bottle counter display](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf16s/).

A [combination unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-gym74/) puts a bubbler and a bottle filler on one pedestal, so you get both in one unit.

## Plan the water quality

A fountain is only as good as what comes into it. Specify an inline filter at each unit, sized for the expected flow, and put filter changes on the maintenance schedule from day one. Write in who changes them and how often. If nobody owns the filter, nobody changes it.

## What the submittal pack should include

Ask every bidder for the same pack so you compare like with like:

- Product datasheet with dimensions, flow rates, materials and connections
- CE declaration of conformity and the manufacturer's quality management certificate
- Hygiene or drinking water approval for the materials in contact with water
- Installation guide with the fixing and plumbing details
- Warranty terms and the local service arrangement
- Lead time to site, by model

If a bidder cannot produce these quickly, that tells you something about the support you will get in year three. Our [technical library](https://aquelon.com/library/) holds catalogues, certifications and our warranty policy, with installation guides on request.

## The short version

Count outlets by where pupils gather. Chill the water. Match the steel to the site. Specify for abuse. Make every location accessible. Put bottle fillers in the mix. Own the filters.

Get those right in the tender and the fountains stop being the line that bites you.

If you are writing a school specification now, [send me the scope](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with a priced quote within one working day.

## Sources

- International Code Council, "2021 International Plumbing Code, Table 403.1 Minimum Number of Required Plumbing Fixtures", 2021. https://codes.iccsafe.org/s/IPC2021P1/chapter-4-fixtures-faucets-and-fixture-fittings/IPC2021P1-Ch04-Sec403.1
- US Access Board, "ADA Accessibility Standards, section 602 Drinking Fountains". https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602
- Australian Stainless Steel Development Association, "316: The First Step Up". https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up
